foreign_nationals.note: Three official counts taken on different dates by different agencies; they do not agree. India is the largest single nationality reported, revised upward from 178 to 288 across updates.

notes: The headline figure is bodies recovered, not identified deaths. Only about 4% of the roughly 900 bodies found by 1 September had been formally identified; forensic teams from India, China, Japan, Singapore and South Korea were still working as of 7 September.
Missing is a separate category and is not presumed dead. NDRRMA's own language treats these people as unlocated, and the count is not additive with bodies recovered without that caveat.

District counts reflect where a body was found, not where the person lived or died. Bodies travelled up to 240 km downstream, which is why Chitwan (363) and the two Nawalparasi districts (445 combined) show higher recovered-body counts than the upstream epicentre districts of Rasuwa and Nuwakot.
The often-quoted ~900 figure is the 31 August snapshot, not a competing method. It is the same count at an earlier date.
No consolidated official injured count was published after 31 August 2026, and no national displaced-household total was found on any primary government page.

summary.text: All wards reported inaccessible by road as of 1 September. Only ward 1 had grid power as of 6 September; four wards remained dark. Site of the Upper Trishuli-1 project.
Grid power restored on 7 September. Contains Mailung, reachable only by helicopter as of 8 September, and the Upper Trishuli 3A and 3B sites.

Twenty-four bodies were found in a single house at Betrawati (ward 10). Between Sole Bazar and Akkare Bazar in ward 7 houses were washed away, two concrete bridges destroyed and more than 200 residents were out of contact. Nearly all wards had grid power back by 6 September; the town water supply was running on a 100 kVA diesel generator.
Site of the Trishuli Galchhi project. No municipality-level casualty or damage figure published.
Parts of the municipality had received no humanitarian assistance as of 1 September.
Nepal Telecom restored its Kispang site by 1 September using helicopter-carried technicians. No municipality-level casualty figure published.
Two bridges on the Tadi Khola were destroyed.

The Prithvi Highway is fully blocked at Krishnabhir where about 70 m of road foundation collapsed into the Trishuli. The Muglin-Kathmandu section is closed both directions; about half of a 300 m bypass track had opened by early September before new slope cracks were found above the worksite. The Phurke Khola bridge at Malekhu was also washed away.
Hub of the reopened right-bank detour that restores a rough single-lane connection to Trishuli Bazar without crossing the destroyed river bridges.
Downstream municipality on the Trishuli. No municipality-level figure published; Chitwan's 363 recovered bodies are a district total and reflect where remains were found, not local deaths.
Downstream municipality on the Narayani. No municipality-level figure published.

grid.detail: Completely destroyed and buried under landslide debris. Not restored as of the latest reporting, and cited as a key evacuation bottleneck.
Used by NEA to reroute power, stepped down to 11 kV for local feeders. Active and carrying emergency restoration load.
Not detailed in the sources checked; damage is implied by the destruction of the Chilime powerhouse but no figure was published.

restoration.note: Nepal Energy Forum gives 83% for the same date; the two are not reconciled.
OnlineKhabar separately reports about 90% for the same date.
About 120 families still without power. The Kathmandu Post described this as nearly all households on 6 September.

restoration.detail: 500 portable 2 kW household solar units and 13 institutional solar systems distributed through the Alternative Energy Promotion Centre; 1,268 vulnerable Rasuwa households flagged for solar.

impact.text: Nepal became a net electricity exporter for the first time in about a decade in the fiscal year ending mid-July 2026, earning Rs 18.75 bn from sales to India and Bangladesh. Officials expect that to reverse in the winter low-flow season and have sought advance import approvals from India effective September 2026.
India agreed to supply advance power to Nepal to cope with the flood, ahead of the normal schedule.

Loss estimates diverge sharply. IPPAN puts hydropower-sector losses at Rs 25-30 bn, roughly a quarter to a third of affected project costs; NEA's preliminary assessment says hundreds of billions of rupees; the Finance Minister attributed Rs 100 bn specifically to hydro infrastructure within a Rs 900 bn economy-wide rebuilding figure.

Missing-worker counts across the energy sector were revised sharply downward as rescue and contact efforts progressed: 933 (NDRRMA), 898 at 11 projects (IPPAN, 29 August), 983 out of contact against 639 officially counted missing, and by 7 September the Nepal Army believed 121 people were still trapped in hydropower tunnels.

road.detail: Betrawati-Rasuwagadhi road (42 km) destroyed at multiple points; no reopening date and authorities advise against travel.
Miteri Friendship Bridge and the border customs post destroyed on 26 August.
16 km section toward the China border damaged; market area flood-hit on 26 August. A 75 m Bailey bridge span is needed here.
Bogatitar-Kalikasthan-Dhunche section reopened to light four-wheel-drive only; the Bidur-Dhunche road was limited to small 4WD vehicles.

displacement_site.detail: Relief supplies staged here; onward delivery to villages is the bottleneck.

road.detail: Passable in daylight only, with a mandatory night closure enforced. (unofficial)
Trishuli-Mailung-Syabrubesi road washed away; helicopter access only for relief.
Roads to Simle and Shanti Bazaar wiped out; no access to shops, hospitals or government offices.
Old and new Betrawati bridges swept away and the Trishuli-Betrawati road extensively damaged. A 48 m Bailey bridge is planned but not yet installed.

power.detail: Not reported separately from the Nuwakot district figure.

road.detail: Old and new Trishuli Bazar bridges swept away. A 48 m Bailey bridge is planned but not yet installed.

telecom.detail: Ncell tower still down in the Trishuli/Bidur area.

road.detail: Reachable via the reopened Galchhi detour; the direct Trishuli-Betrawati road is still damaged.

road.detail: Bridge near the Water Resources and Irrigation Division destroyed. The Nepal Army began installing a Bailey bridge; a temporary cable-pulley (tuen) crossing carries people and light goods.
Terminus of the Galchhi detour route toward Trishuli Bazar; open as a narrow single-lane track.
Hub of the reopened right-bank detour road, the alternative to the destroyed Trishuli-corridor bridges.
Phurke Khola bridge washed away, with local road damage.

Prithvi Highway fully blocked at Krishnabhir by a 70 m road-foundation collapse into the Trishuli; the Muglin-Kathmandu section is closed both ways. About 50 m of a 300 m bypass track had opened before new slope cracks were found above the worksite.
All wards reported inaccessible by road.

power.detail: Only ward 1 has power; four wards remain dark.

corridor.text: Pasang Lhamu Highway (NH42), Betrawati to Rasuwagadhi: 42 km damaged at multiple points with several concrete bridges washed away, plus a further 16 km from Syabrubesi toward the China border. No confirmed reopening date; authorities advise against travel to Rasuwagadhi, Timure or Kerung until the route is reassessed.

Prithvi Highway is closed both directions at Krishnabhir in Benighat Rorang, Dhading, where about 70 m of road foundation collapsed into the Trishuli. A 300 m bypass track is under construction, roughly half open, but seven cracks up to 15 m long were found in the slope above the worksite. The Prime Minister said the section would reopen within September.

Detour in use: Galchhi to Kalleritar, Koshikhola, Piplatar, Darshantar, Chhatrekhola and Gauribesi along the right bank of the Trishuli. It restores a rough single-lane connection from Dhading and Galchhi to Trishuli Bazar without crossing the destroyed river bridges, but is narrow, slow and hard for two-way traffic.

Bailey bridges planned by the Department of Roads at four locations: Devighat in Bidur, where the Nepal Army has begun installation; Trishuli Bazaar and Betrawati, each needing about a 48 m span; and Syabrubesi, needing about 75 m. Moving the components is hampered because the lower road sections are still blocked. China has supplied Bailey components at the Korala border for possible use at Rasuwagadhi.

Named bridges destroyed: Betrawati old and new; the Trishuli River bridge at Tupche; Trishuli Bazar old and new; Simchaur; the bridge near the Water Resources and Irrigation Division at Devighat; a Mid-Hill Highway bridge; two on the Tadi Khola; Shreekali, Budhsinghghat, Ratamate and Phosretar over the Trishuli; and in Dhading the Syaltar road bridge, Ghatbesi bridge, Phurke Khola bridge at Malekhu and two on the Kolpu Khola.

Bridge totals are not reconciled across sources. NDRRMA reported 41 motorable bridges washed away and 4 more damaged; OnlineKhabar counted at least 19 bridges and about 40 km of road along the Trishuli corridor; the Department of Roads early estimate was 68 suspension and 33 driveable bridges damaged, with an initial Rs 15 bn estimate for road and bridge infrastructure.

Electricity, district level: Rasuwa 78% of 14,281 affected households restored, Nuwakot 96.7% of 68,679, Dhading 99.8% of 83,642 with about 120 families still dark. Rasuwa floods affected roughly 10% of Nepal's total generation capacity.

Water supply: 55 drinking-water projects damaged across Rasuwa, Nuwakot, Dhading and Gorkha, with Rs 640 m estimated damage; Nuwakot is worst hit with 22 projects affected. The Bidur Water Supply Project runs on a 100 kVA diesel generator distributing about 500,000 litres a day.

UNICEF reported at least 22,000 children in the flood-affected areas without safe drinking water, sanitation and hygiene support, and dispatched supplies for about 19,000 people in Rasuwa and Nuwakot.

Telecommunications: Nepal Telecom restored 116 of 120 affected towers by 1 September using helicopter-carried crews. Ncell restored 24 of 27, leaving Ghattekhola and Timure in Rasuwa and Trishuli/Bidur in Nuwakot down; 60 km of fibre was damaged and total telecom infrastructure damage is put at Rs 450 m.

Displacement: 3,458 people were living in 27 displacement sites in Nuwakot and Rasuwa, mostly in schools, as of 1 September. IOM's Displacement Tracking Matrix covers 15 sites in Dhading, Nuwakot and Rasuwa and estimates 4,288 households affected, of which 2,886 displaced.

Cross-border: the Gyirong checkpoint on the Chinese side was destroyed, along with a 5 km stretch of China National Highway 216 toward Rasuwagadhi, and communications and power to the Gyirong Port area were cut. About 80 trucks and 170 containers were stranded in Gyirong town. On the Nepal side the Rasuwagadhi customs office was destroyed and more than 300 vehicles plus roughly 1,000 electric vehicles awaiting export were swept away.
